paras: The attempted lynching of E. Langley Jones was an incident at Colorado City, Texas, in which a Scurry county posse hunting horse thieves seized Jones, a rancher, and prepared to hang him. He was freed when an Englishman in the posse and the Sheriff proved he had been mistaken for another man. The only known account is Jones's own signed narrative, printed without a date for the incident in the Los Angeles Daily Herald on June 10, 1888.

Jones rode about seventy miles from his Tom Green county ranch to Colorado City each month for supplies. On one trip he rode back to town at dusk for a forgotten errand and was told that a Scurry county posse was out after horse thieves.

Returning in the dark to where he had tied his second horse, Jones was stopped at gunpoint, tied, "collared and kicked" and thrown across a saddle. Asked for their authority, his two captors said they would show it at the next cross-bar, a gate beam used for hanging horse thieves.

In town they held him in a saloon so the rest of the posse could see him "strung up." Jones persuaded an Englishman among the returning men to compare his horses' brands with those of the stolen stock. As the posse dragged him out, the Englishman returned with the Sheriff, who convinced the men that Jones was not the horse thief Alf. Harris.
Jones was released with what he called "off-hand apologies," and the posse then insisted that he buy the drinks. No report of any charge against the posse appears in the coverage.

The Los Angeles Daily Herald ran the story on page 3 as a signed personal sketch headed "NEARLY LYNCHED." with the subhead "How a Man was Mistaken for a Horse-Thief-What Came of It." Jones called his captors "self-made deputies" who "went it blind," while explaining that horse stealing in "the wild southwest" was "deemed worthy of the death penalty." No other newspaper account of the incident appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of E. Langley Jones
bases: A posse hunting horse thieves seized the narrator, said it would hang him at a cross-bar, and was dragging him out of a saloon to do so when the Sheriff stopped it, an attempted lynching in which no one died (A1).
The narrator says a group of posse men acting without lawful process, whom he calls "self-made deputies," meant to hang him as a horse thief, but he was freed alive, so no killing occurred (A1).
The only account is the victim's own signed, undated first-person narrative in the Los Angeles daily herald; no Texas report or other paper was found (A1).

accounts.label: Victim's first-person narrative
accounts.gist: Jones says a Scurry county posse seized him in the dark, tied and kicked him, and was dragging him out of a Colorado City saloon to hang him when the Sheriff and an Englishman of the posse proved he was not the horse thief Alf. Harris.

framing.detail: Headlined "NEARLY LYNCHED."; told as a personal adventure that calls the captors "self-made deputies" who "went it blind" while stating that horse stealing in "the wild southwest" is "deemed worthy of the death penalty."

record_check.dossier: Not given; only the print date 1888-06-10 is known, and the narrative is retrospective, so the incident may predate 1888.
Not stated for Colorado City; posse from Scurry county, victim's ranch in Tom Green county.
Seizure at gunpoint, binding, kicking, and an interrupted attempt to hang; "beating" overstates a collaring and kicking, and "pursuit" was of horse thieves generally, not of the victim.
A posse from Scurry county hunting horse thieves; members unnamed.
Not stated; he calls himself a countryman of an Englishman in the posse.

record_check.record: ...a countryman and the sheriff proved mistaken identity.
record_check.dossier: Supported, but it is a single, undated first-person narrative from the victim.

info: Not given; the narrative was printed 1888-06-10 and describes a past incident at an unstated date, beginning about two hours before sundown on a monthly supply trip.
Seized at a hitching spot about nine or ten miles out on the road from Colorado City; held in a saloon in the lower end of Colorado City.
E. Langley Jones, the narrator, a rancher from Tom Green county; race not stated; he calls himself a countryman of an Englishman in the posse.
Taken for a horse thief; mistaken for "a noted young horse-thief named Alf. Harris".
A posse from Scurry county hunting horse thieves; two captors, later joined by "the rest of the posse"; the narrator calls them "self-made deputies" and "the gang".
Released with "off-hand apologies"; the posse then insisted he buy drinks; he says his nerves kept him in town three weeks.

sources.note: "NEARLY LYNCHED." Signed first-person narrative by E. Langley Jones: seized by a Scurry county posse hunting horse thieves, taken to a Colorado City saloon, nearly hanged until an Englishman and the Sheriff proved mistaken identity. No date of the incident.
quotes: they would show me their authority when they reached the next cross-bar
the boys were dragging me out of the saloon for the crowning act of the drama, when my countryman rushed up with the Sheriff
It seems that I had been taken for a noted young horse-thief named Alf. Harris
In the usual devil-may-care way peculiar to the southwest, the self-made deputies in my case "went it blind."

set_aside: Los Angeles County Supervisors' minutes: E. Langley Jones made clerk of Justice King's court; no link to the Texas episode stated.
City Council minutes: Justice King asks that his clerk E. Langley Jones be put on the salary roll; no link to the Texas episode stated.
